source_refs.note: Strain: a main subheading of 5.3 Stress, strain and Young's modulus, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 96-96.

blocks.text: Strain is a measure of the deformation of a solid when stress is applied to it. In the case of deformation in one dimension, strain is defined as the fractional change in length. If ΔL is the change in length and L₀ is the original length (Fig. 5.3 (a), then strain is given by

blocks.alt: A pink bar of length L is pulled by a force F at each end, the arrows pointing outward. Dotted outlines beyond both ends show how far the bar is stretched.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.3(a): Tensile strain (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.3(a)).

blocks.text_alt: Strain (ε) = Change in length (ΔL) / Original length (L₀)   (5.2)

blocks.text: Since strain is the ratio of lengths, it is dimensionless and therefore, has no units. If strain ε is due to tensile stress σ, it is called tensile strain, and if it is produced as a result of compressive stress σ, it is termed as compressive strain.

blocks.caption: Figure 5.3(b): Volumetric strain (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.3(b)).

blocks.title: For Your Information
blocks.text: Although it is named after the 19th century British Scientist Thomas Young, the concept was developed in 1727 by Leonhard Euler.
